red.summary: Duties can encourage safer behavior by making certain conduct required or prohibited. Learn to distinguish the legal rule from the economic reasons someone might obey it.
checklist: I can identify an obligation and its enforcement consequence
I can explain a simple incentive
I can recognize nonfinancial motivations to comply

sections.title: Rules Change Choices
sections.body_md: A building code requires working fire exits. An owner may comply because of inspection penalties, concern for occupants, reputation, or professional responsibility. Economics studies how incentives shape choices, while law determines whether the obligation exists. A legal analyst should not reduce every human motive to money. The key comparison is between what the rule requires and whether its enforcement and surrounding institutions make safe conduct more likely.

sections.title: Prevention May Cost Less Than Repair
sections.body_md: A shop can spend money maintaining a stair rail or risk injuring customers and facing legal consequences. The owner should consider the probability and seriousness of harm alongside prevention costs, but the governing legal duty cannot always be determined by this calculation alone. Safety legislation or professional standards may impose mandatory requirements. Economic reasoning helps explain incentives; it does not authorize breaking a binding rule because noncompliance seems cheaper.

sections.title: Who Bears the Risk?
sections.body_md: If a company can pass all injury costs to customers or neighbors, its private decision may ignore wider harm. Rules assigning responsibility or requiring precautions can change that incentive. A good learner identifies whose conduct creates risk, who suffers if precautions fail, and which institution sets the standard. Law helps organize cooperation by protecting people who may never have entered a voluntary contract with the actor causing danger.

yellow.focus: Analyze negligence incentives and the cost of accidents
yellow.summary: Learn a simple expected-harm framework for understanding precautions. Distinguish efficient risk reduction from the legal standard of care imposed by a particular jurisdiction.
checklist: I can calculate a simple probability-weighted harm conceptually
I can identify when precaution changes expected loss
I can distinguish economic model from governing negligence law

sections.title: Probability and Severity Both Matter
sections.body_md: A poorly secured ladder has a low chance of falling on any one day, but a severe injury could result. Expected harm combines probability and the magnitude of loss. A reasonable preventive measure might reduce either. The economic question is whether the expected reduction justifies the cost, while the legal question asks whether the governing duty of care requires that measure. These questions may be related but are not always identical. Law can also protect interests that cannot be fully priced.

sections.title: The Cost of Care Has Limits
sections.body_md: The Hand formula, associated with a US negligence decision, compares the burden of precaution with the probability and gravity of loss in a particular doctrinal setting. It is not a universal negligence test used in every country or claim. The formula can make trade-offs clearer, but real cases involve uncertainty about estimates and nonmonetary interests. The lawyer should use it as an analytical aid when applicable law permits, not as a substitute for statutory or judicial standards.

sections.title: Rules May Affect Both Sides
sections.body_md: Liability rules can influence how firms prevent accidents and how potential victims take precautions. Comparative fault rules, insurance and information can change those incentives, though their effects depend on actual human behavior and legal design. A simplified economic model should state its assumptions before predicting outcomes. It should also avoid blaming victims merely because they could have taken a costly precaution. Responsibility remains a question of law, evidence and justice.

orange.focus: Examine externalities, principal-agent problems and regulatory compliance
orange.summary: Complex institutions can have incentives that diverge from the interests of clients, workers or the public. Analyze how legal duties and monitoring address such problems under real-world constraints.
checklist: I can explain moral hazard in regulated activities
I can compare liability and regulatory mechanisms

sections.title: The Agent May Not Share the Principal's Goals
sections.body_md: A manager is rewarded for rapid production while owners value long-term safety and customers need reliable products. This is a principal-agent problem: an agent's incentives can diverge from those of the person or institution for whom they act. Contracts, oversight, liability and professional duties may reduce the gap, but none is perfect. A legal analyst must identify the actual duties and authority of each person rather than assuming every organizational mistake is one individual's moral failure.

sections.title: Insurance Can Change Behavior
sections.body_md: If an actor expects an insurer or public fund to bear most accident costs, the actor's incentive to take care might weaken. Economists call this potential moral hazard. Insurance arrangements can also support necessary risk-taking and protect victims, so the concept is not an argument against insurance itself. Legal duties, deductibles, monitoring and regulatory standards may affect behavior. The correct analysis examines actual incentives and empirical effects, not a simplistic assumption that insured people act recklessly.

sections.title: Regulation and Liability Serve Different Roles
sections.body_md: A regulator can set preventive standards before harm occurs, while private liability may compensate or deter after a legally recognized injury. Each method has costs: monitoring may be difficult, and litigation can be expensive or uncertain. Hybrid approaches may work better. An advanced analysis considers who possesses information, who can act promptly, who is vulnerable and which institution has lawful authority. The best legal design addresses risk without placing an impossible burden on affected individuals.

black.focus: Design duty rules that internalize risk without sacrificing fairness
black.summary: At doctoral depth, evaluate whether economic incentives can improve safety while preserving nonnegotiable rights and proportional responsibility. Defend an institutionally realistic mix of rules.
checklist: I can critique purely monetary approaches to duties
I can design proportionate preventive and remedial incentives
I can evaluate distribution and accountability of institutional risk

sections.title: Not Every Harm Has a Market Price
sections.body_md: A firm might calculate that paying compensation is cheaper than preventing a certain class of injury. The calculation can help identify incentives, but law may impose nonwaivable duties because lives and dignity cannot be treated as ordinary inventory. A doctoral analysis distinguishes efficiency as a descriptive or policy criterion from the institution's legal authority to enforce safety standards. It must ask who bears the risk, who can prevent it, and whether monetary damages adequately protect affected persons.

A doctoral analysis distinguishes efficiency as a descriptive or policy criterion from the institution's legal authority to enforce safety standards. It must ask who bears the risk, who can prevent it, and whether monetary damages adequately protect affected persons.

sections.title: Optimal Incentives Depend on Information
sections.body_md: A regulator may lack detailed information about every workplace hazard, while firms may have incentives to conceal unsafe practices. Private litigation can uncover some evidence but may miss diffuse harms. An effective scheme could combine mandatory reporting, targeted inspection, proportionate penalties and private remedies where legally appropriate. Each component creates administrative and distributive costs. A doctoral design states assumptions about detection probability, compliance behavior and vulnerability instead of claiming that one perfect penalty solves everything.

sections.title: Safety and Justice Are Joint Objectives
sections.body_md: A policy that reduces average accident costs could still concentrate danger in low-income neighborhoods or among precarious workers. Evaluation should consider those distributions and protected rights. An institutionally legitimate system needs clear duties, reliable enforcement, opportunities to challenge mistakes and accessible compensation for proven wrongs. Economic analysis is most useful when it makes hidden risks visible while refusing to treat people as expendable variables in an aggregate calculation.
